speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS, therefore, reviews the Banking Act from time to time to ensure that the regulatory framework for banks continues to foster safety and soundness in Singapore's banking system while making sure that requirements are not unduly burdensome.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this round of amendments, MAS is changing two long-standing regulatory practices which have lost relevance over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This DBU-ACU divide has traditionally been used to distinguish the domestic and offshore operations of banks and merchant banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill will also make other amendments to enhance MAS' regulatory and supervisory powers to tackle new and emerging risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include expanding the grounds for revoking bank licences and introducing new powers for MAS to impose requirements on outsourcing arrangements of banks and merchant banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will now go through the main amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has engaged the industry extensively on the proposed amendments and has taken into consideration their feedback on the implementation timeline.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: DBU and ACU have their origins in the creation of the Asian Dollar Market in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Like the Euro market located in London, the Asian Dollar Market served as a major source of funding for investment, trading and risk-management needs for the region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The DBU is used to book domestic transactions, which are mostly denominated in the Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ACU is used to book offshore transactions and these are denominated in foreign currency.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS' regulatory requirements for banks and merchant banks, in turn, apply depending on whether the activity was booked in DBU or ACU.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Foreign banks that wished to participate in the Asian Dollar Market through their ACU had to meet high standards of admission and have reputable home regulators exercising oversight of their global operations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those that also engaged in domestic businesses in Singapore through the DBU were then subject to additional prudential requirements from MAS, such as limits on large exposure and equity investment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The DBU-ACU divide provided a way to safeguard domestic financial stability, without unduly impinging on the growth of offshore banking activities conducted out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also provided a simple basis for awarding developmental incentives to encourage the growth of offshore banking activities out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While the DBU-ACU divide has served us well for decades, it is no longer relevant and will be removed because of the following reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, regulatory reforms since the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) have put all banks around the world on a sounder footing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These developments mean that there is less need to distinguish between banks' offshore and domestic banking activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Global regulators have also agreed on a common framework to control large exposures to a single counterparty or a group of connected counterparties, limiting these exposures to 25% of Tier 1 capital.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, MAS has also enhanced its regulatory framework over time which has made the divide less meaningful.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, banks in Singapore are required to meet liquidity requirements based on all-currency and Singapore dollar criteria, rather than DBU or ACU.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has also introduced the framework for domestic systemically important banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Designated banks are subject to additional supervisory measures covering both their domestic and offshore businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, a lot has changed in terms of the regulatory environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Globally, you have higher standards now after GFC that covers all banks, offshore as well as onshore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the third reason is MAS' developmental incentives have also broadened.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the past, MAS' incentives were focused on ACU to encourage the growth of offshore banking activities out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, MAS assesses the developmental merits of an activity much more broadly and no longer based on domestic versus offshore distinction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a result, the DBU-ACU divide is no longer useful and will impose a compliance burden on banks with little benefits to prudential soundness or systemic stability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will rely on the consolidated supervision by these banks' home supervisors to manage such risks at the bank group level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second amendment is the consolidation of merchant banks' regulation into the Banking Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Merchant banks are a class of financial institutions approved under the MAS Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unlike banks, merchant banks are not allowed to accept deposits or raise funds in Singapore dollar from the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, when merchant banks were first introduced in Singapore in the 1970s, they engaged primarily in capital market services, such as corporate finance and fund management.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They were, therefore, subject to a less stringent approval regime under the MAS Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Subsequently, we encouraged merchant banks to participate in the Asian Dollar Market, by allowing them to apply to operate an ACU for their foreign currency activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They were then subject to certain requirements in the Banking Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Merchant banks have since been subject, therefore, to two pieces of legislation, namely, the MAS Act as an approved financial institution and then by the Banking Act by virtue of their ACU activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The third amendment, the Bill will also introduce new or revised provisions to strengthen MAS' regulatory oversight of banks and merchant banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As these rules apply to both banks and merchant banks, I will refer to them collectively as banks in this section.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, expand grounds for revocation of bank licence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In line with the international regulatory standards and practice, MAS has the power to revoke bank licences under certain circumstances, such as when a bank (a) is carrying on its business in a manner likely to be detrimental to the interests of the depositors of the bank; (b) is contravening the provisions of the Banking Act; or (c) in the case of a foreign bank branch in Singapore, has had its licence in its home jurisdiction withdrawn by its parent supervisory authority.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As our banking landscape changes, new risks emerge, and our regulatory framework has to evolve to better manage these risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the three new grounds are as follows.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, contraventions of provisions of the MAS Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The MAS Act contains important regulatory requirements, such as those relating to anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism, of which non-compliance is regarded as a very severe breach of our regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, in the case of a foreign-owned bank incorporated in Singapore, when the parent bank's licence is withdrawn by the parent supervisory authority.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is in recognition that foreign banks are increasingly operating in Singapore through subsidiaries instead of just branches.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It mirrors the current power MAS has over foreign bank branches today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three, when MAS regards that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a ground that is currently available for revocation for most other financial institutions regulated by MAS, but not for banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This additional ground is also in line with practices in other international jurisdictions, such as Australia and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next, the Bill enhances MAS’ oversight of certain services, such as outsourcing services obtained by banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When banks enter into outsourcing arrangements, MAS expects the bank to maintain the same risk management standards as if the services were performed by the bank itself.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes similar standards and practices in ensuring customer information is safeguarded.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill will enhance MAS' oversight over outsourcing arrangements by introducing a new section 47A in the Banking Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has considered the practices in other leading jurisdictions in setting out these requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These powers are practised in Australia and the European Union (EU).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are timely in light of the increased prevalence and complexity of banks' outsourcing arrangements today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill will provide for the powers and MAS will be consulting on the detailed regulations in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, in line with global regulatory standards, some of the key prudential requirements imposed by MAS include requiring banks to have a stable and sustainable funding structure for their activities and to address risks arising from related-party transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These requirements are currently issued under a general provision in the Banking Act, unlike other important requirements, such as minimum capital requirements which are issued under specific Banking Act provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill will formalise MAS' current powers and raise the signature of these two requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, banks in Singapore are permitted to disclose customer information only in certain specified circumstances, such as when the customer has provided written consent, pursuant to Court orders, or to the bank's external auditor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments, which update the Banking Act, have been through two rounds of public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MAS has also published a detailed response to the feedback received on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the transparency and rigour of MAS' consultation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened that, increasingly, we not just see public consultations on Bills but also detailed responses on the feedback we received.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In response to a question on when MAS would consider it to be in the public interest to revoke a bank licence, MAS responded that it will consider the factors set out in the MAS' Enforcement Monograph.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes whether there was ineffective governance, widespread control failures, pervasive non-compliance, gross misconduct, or serious breaches of applicable law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Enforcement Monograph is a guidance document that is not strictly legally binding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Revoking a bank licence is a very drastic step and, yet, the considerations stated in the Enforcement Monograph are not legally binding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also confirm it will only revoke bank licences on the ground of "public interest" for the most serious cases of ineffective governance, widespread control failures, pervasive non-compliance, gross misconduct, or serious breaches of applicable law, as stated in the Enforcement Monograph?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The definition of "fit and proper" is set out in MAS' Guidelines on Fit and Proper Criteria.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify why, compared to section 15B where key appointment holders, 20% controllers, 12% controllers and indirect controllers of designated financial institutions have to be approved by MAS but under the new section 57FD, only key appointment holders and 20% controllers of credit card or charge card licensees have to be approved by MAS?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share how actively the "fit and proper" requirement is enforced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Have there been individuals that have been denied appointment or removed from their roles for not meeting the "fit and proper" requirement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the new section 27(2) sets out a list of related parties that are subject to MAS' requirements on related-party transactions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes at section 27(2)(e) "any person in a senior management group of the bank".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In response to a question on the definition of an "executive officer", MAS replied that the definition of an "executive officer" is not meant to be descriptive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, MAS expects banks to assess and identify their executive officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also stated that it is good practice for the bank to document how it determines the list of "executive officer(s)".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MAS is seeking to increase its oversight of banks; yet, the strengthened regulations could very easily be circumvented by the banks' own definition of "executive officer".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems strange that we have gone to the effort of strengthening our regulations only to leave the final necessary step in the hands of the banks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would be preferable to leaving it open-ended and subjected to interpretation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It also seeks to consolidate the licensing and regulation of merchant banks under the Banking Act, in an effort to update and strengthen our regulatory framework in light of international and industry developments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, there is one significant and glaring development that we must talk about in updating the Banking Act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Severe floods have ravaged much of Jakarta last week.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With the growing prevalence of the climate-induced events in the world and specifically to our region, there is an urgent need to safeguard financial assets, yet be innovative in legislative interventions to reduce future risks to Singapore's banking industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Do not take my word for it, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Network for Greening our Financial System (NGFS) formed by a group of central bankers and supervisors worldwide, noted that climate risks, I quote, "could be larger, more widespread and diverse" than any other structural change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given that it will come from all sectors and geographies, it is clear our financial system is exposed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Regulatory frameworks around climate-related risk management will allow for a systematic adoption of practices for the accelerated transition towards a sustainable banking sector.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a founding member of NGFS, MAS must lead and contribute in this area.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech on "Green Finance for a Sustainable World" last November, Minister Ong Ye Kung highlighted three key areas to build a financial industry resilient to climate change risks, namely, measuring, mitigating and disclosing these risks.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I agree broadly with the identified areas but the devil, as we know, is in the details.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We know that bookkeeping carbon emissions produced by assets on a bank' balance sheet is always a challenge.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, here in Singapore, existing avenues, such as the Carbon Pricing Act, already allows banks to obtain carbon emissions-related data and estimate their borrower's exposure to carbon regulation and transition risks.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We should institute this so that our banks have clear and comparable data to measure the risk exposure of their public-listed clients.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a former corporate banker myself, I would even push for data collection beyond just carbon emissions data.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our bankers must also obtain information from borrowers to understand where business value could be at risk.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The 2011 floods in Thailand are a critical example of how risks could be embedded in the supply chain and may not be obvious through a carbon data metric.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Operating loss from the floods incurred by Toyota and Honda increased by 37% and 55% respectively in 2011.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change risk has a long-tail and is widespread.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Credit risk metrics have historically been insufficient in addressing tail-end risks.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Metrics that simply average potential risk across multiple years underestimate potential impact.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Solely focusing on high-carbon assets is a good first step but is still insufficient.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Stress testing portfolio risk is also an important part of risk management.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Stress test scenarios should be centrally-developed, not individually designed, to ensure that there is alignment to the Paris Agreement target and geographically-relevant worst-case scenarios.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must applaud Singapore banks for moving quickly in announcing policies to cease financing new coal power plants.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Two out of three banks will not be increasing their exposure to the transition risks of this industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As more large banks and insurers decide to divest from coal power development, banks that continue to consider such projects are exposed to increasing risks that will be harder to mitigate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the Association of Banks in Singapore has Responsible Banking Guidelines and a haze toolkit, these are voluntary standards.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Bangladesh already has a mandatory environmental risk management guideline for Bangladeshi banks.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mandatory standards in Singapore and international alignment are key signposts that our banking industry is robustly equipped to mitigate environmental, social and governance risks, particularly around climate change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As this Bill considers the publication requirements of banks under clause 12, we should also consider the disclosure of climate risks.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Governor of the Bank of England said that "to bring climate risks and resilience into the heart of financial decision-making, climate disclosure must become comprehensive".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Commonwealth Bank of Australia was sued for misleading investors by failing to disclose climate-related risks in its 2016 annual report.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), Singapore's recent review of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Sustainable Banking Regulations, only Malaysia has firmly expected banks to assess, mitigate and publicly disclose their portfolio-level exposure to material environmental and social (E&S) risks, including climate risk and information on transactions assessed/escalated/approved with conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore should be requiring our banks to do the same.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Accounting for climate risks is hard work, but there are existing networks like the Pilot Project by UN Environment Programme Finance Institute (UNEP-FI) on Implementing Recommendations by the Taskforce for Climate Financial Disclosures (TCFD) as well as the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF) that can support our banks in this process.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will we consider a timeline for mandatory TCFD disclosures for financial industries as well as listed companies, since voluntary regimes are typically not useful in generating comparable and usable industry-wide information?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Minister looking at a supervisory engagement roadmap on climate change?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will MAS support the banking industry with centrally-developed stress test scenarios that incorporate the views of experts and civil society?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Minister consider leading an ASEAN taskforce that embarks on a bottom-up modelling of business risks from climate change across our region, including the supply chain impacts across borders?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond this being a business opportunity, accelerating the growth of green finance reduces instability to our financial system in the future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While our banks have been highly positive on the green finance opportunities, there is still much we can do.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A number of countries have established national green banks to provide initial funding to develop clean energy, transport, energy-efficient markets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Green Bank Network, based out of Washington DC, currently consists of 15 national, state or city level member banks that aim to catalyse green financing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This includes the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (CEFC) of Australia.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) government seeded the UK Green Investment Bank in 2012 that continues to deploy green capital successfully.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The financial industry has been all abuzz with the opening of five digital bank licences by MAS.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In our licensing considerations for these digital banks, we have made provisions to enable new players that have regional reach and diverse customer bases.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, incentivise and harness the innovative essence of these new digital partnerships not only to encourage the collection and use of new data but also to create new sustainable financing solutions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, ING Real Estate Finance and a partner launched ING REF Sustainable App in 2016.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Within two years, it helped identify €35 million of potential energy cost savings within its real estate portfolio.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister please clarify if sustainable finance will be a key component of our digital bank roadmap for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong noted in his recent New Year message that "A Singapore turned inward cannot survive".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, we are and always will be an open economy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Its indirect contribution fuelling the rest of the economy is clearly way more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given what we now know of climate change and its impact from science and data, we absolutely cannot let such risks build up with little or no visibility.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Large institutional investors like Aviva Investors share the same view.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Its Chief Investment Officer said recently, quote "understanding climate risk isn’t an exercise in trying to save species and habitats; this is also about protecting people's retirement income and their investments." Smart regulation has allowed MAS to be nimble and adaptable as a world-class regulator and central bank.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must act with the fierce urgency of now.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarifications on what I have outlined above and his assurance that MAS' regulatory roadmap is running alongside, if not ahead of, this climate crisis so as to build a climate-change resilient, robust and responsible financial industry for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the considerations for revoking a bank licence on the ground of public interest are not set out in legislation, given that revocation is a drastic step.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng also sought confirmation that MAS would only revoke bank licences on the ground of public interest for the most serious of cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Revoking a bank licence is, indeed, a very drastic measure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS is very cognisant that it is the most severe regulatory action that it can take with respect to a bank.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS, therefore, has a strong and inherent incentive to use this power judiciously, as a licence revocation means the bank will have to stop business, affecting its customers as well as other stakeholders, such as shareholders and employees.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it is not done right, or not based on strong grounds, it will affect our credibility and reputation as a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, as far as possible, MAS has set out specific grounds on which it may revoke a bank licence in the Banking Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include situations where a bank has contravened the Banking Act or is carrying on its business in a manner likely to be detrimental to its depositors' interest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In all cases, MAS will consider the circumstances for licence revocations set out in the Enforcement Monograph, which provides guidance to the industry on the underlying principles guiding MAS' use of enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That said, as the banking sector will continue to evolve, it is not possible to anticipate all circumstances under which MAS may revoke a bank licence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The ground of public interest thus provides MAS with the option to take timely action in unanticipated circumstances to protect the public interest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also considered at that time the wider public interest in closing these banks in order to safeguard Singapore's reputation as a clean and trusted financial centre and to send a strong deterrent message that such breaches and misconduct will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have mentioned earlier that the public interest ground is in line with practices in other jurisdictions, such as Australia and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This ground is also not unique to banks, as MAS already has the same revocation power on public interest grounds for other classes of financial institutions it currently supervises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next set of questions relates to the powers for MAS to approve 20% controllers and key appointment holders, and to remove key appointment holders, of credit card or charge card licensees.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the approval requirements for credit card or charge card licensees differ from that of banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS calibrates its licensing and regulatory requirements to be commensurate with the risks posed by financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Credit and charge card licensees conduct limited business activities, while banks conduct a wider range of activities, such as deposit-taking and lending, in addition to credit and charge card issuance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, the thresholds for MAS to approve controllers and key appointment holders are tiered accordingly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng also requested more information on the enforcement of the "fit and proper" requirement by MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The requirement is an essential component of MAS' regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Applicants must declare their fitness and propriety when they apply for MAS' approval.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS conducts checks on these individuals before approval and may take action to remove such individuals where necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether MAS would consider prescribing a list of executive officers in subsidiary legislation to prevent banks from circumventing MAS' requirements on related-party transactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Mr Louis Ng has rightly pointed out, an executive officer of a bank in Singapore and his or her family members would be considered as related parties of the bank. "Executive officer", in relation to a bank, is already defined in section 2 of the Banking Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This qualitative definition is familiar to the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The term is also used in other sections of the Banking Act as well as other MAS-administered legislation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This approach is preferred to a listing of job titles or designations as it is able to better capture persons holding managerial roles and responsibilities and is less likely to be affected by differences in nomenclature among banks or changes in specific designations over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, if we are too definitive in spelling out all the designations, our worry is, it makes it even easier to circumvent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is much better that the industry, which already understands the definition, live by the definition and the spirit of the definition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS assesses that the risk of circumvention now, based on the banking industry's understanding of the definition, is low, given the common understanding of the scope of an executive officer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These issues are actually not within the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will, nevertheless, respond briefly to them in this session.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will be happy to address them in greater detail on other suitable occasions, such through a Parliamentary Question or the upcoming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore's financial sector can play a decisive role in promoting sustainable development opportunities and powering this transition, especially in Asia.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Finance, innovation and technology together can be a force for good, to overcome challenges and address climate change.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To be a leading centre for Green Finance in Asia and globally, MAS is taking steps that are very in line with what Ms Anthea Ong has spoken about, namely, first, build financial system resilience to environmental risk; and second, develop green finance solutions and markets.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But green financing has the potential to be a mainstream activity of all traditional banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, yes, we are embarking on an engagement process with the industry and the public starting with this consultation paper in the first quarter of this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS is also working to anchor green expertise in Singapore, such as Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) researchers and investment analysts from asset managers, through mandates under the Green Investment Programme, as well as professional service providers that conduct ESG rating, assurance and certification of green financing solutions, through various grants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will promote the adoption of green financing solutions, such as green bonds and loans, through all these measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In assessing the digital bank applications, MAS will be looking at how they can contribute to sustainable financing, which is a key growth strategy for Singapore's financial sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Looking at the potential tenderers, I am sure many of them will also be eager to portray and present their green credentials to MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These initiatives will support the mobilisation of resources to activities that promote sustainable development in Asia and globally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.
